While using photometry from stellar events to analyze the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for aerosol depth measurements is remarkably delicate. Building upon our previous work, we have significantly enhanced the accuracy of aerosol depth calculations by employing a more precise method that takes into account the systematic errors associated with using stellar spectrum models. This new approach allows for determining the aerosol depth at a specific altitude or using a model that is free from assumptions about its value, thereby eliminating the need for prior knowledge. To further improve the accuracy, we propose using a combination of two distinct stellar events: a bright UV event and a less intense optical event. This proposal is particularly significant for using photometry from stellar events to analyze the atmosphere, given the impending arrival of the LSST survey that will feature a greatly increased sensitivity to optical events but a decreased sensitivity to UV events. Thanks to the IMF-based spectrum model, we are able to determine the source of the stellar event's spectrum, whether from the main sequence or a giant phase, which is crucial for applying the new method or the one from our previous work. We demonstrate the efficacy of our enhanced technique by applying it to data from two distinct stellar events observed by the Eu:LLR instrument during the 2019-2020 aerosol event in Santiago, Chile. As a result, we are able to determine the aerosol depth at a height of 0-10km to a precision of 0.01, which we then use to compare our results with those obtained using the EU:LLA instrument and the GOMOS instrument on the Aura and Envisat satellites. Finally, we propose using this new technique to create a global map of aerosol depth at a precision of 0.01 by employing a network of stellar photometry instruments in space. Such a map would be extremely valuable in validating the accuracy of satellite-based aerosol depth measurements and would also provide a critical input for using photometry from stellar events to analyze the atmosphere in atmospheric models. Alternatively, this new technique could be used to improve the accuracy of aerosol depth calculations using existing satellite instruments, which would then be free to be used to study other atmospheric phenomena. Finally, we believe that this new technique could also be applied to analyzing the atmosphere using photometry from non-stellar events, such as the giant flare that occurred in 2020, which could provide a much-needed check on the accuracy of atmospheric models.

Specifically, for group-based data, constructing meaningful features involves representing group actions in a way that machine learning models can utilize them effectively. A promising approach in this area is the use of wreath products of groups, which offers a rich framework for feature engineering but presents computational challenges due to the high dimensionality of feature vectors. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called the Cartesian Partition Method, which provides an efficient way to calculate the distribution of features based on the representation of groups in wreath products. This method is particularly useful for identifying features that are significantly distributed among distinct group actions, which are crucial for developing efficient machine learning models. We further illustrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a variety of theoretical scenarios and a real-world dataset from the Human Connectome Project, which involves analyzing brain signal integration patterns. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the Cartesian Partition Method in reducing feature dimensions substantially while preserving the underlying group-based structure, which paves the way for applying standard machine learning algorithms to this data. This research provides a comprehensive framework for representing groups in wreath products, which offers a valuable resource for researchers working in this area and provides a foundation for developing effective machine learning models for analyzing group-based data. Beyond describing these models, the review also examines the theoretical frameworks they align with, highlighting the need for clear categorization based on model structure and epidemiological context. This viewpoint identifies the use of compartmental models that incorporate non-linear incidence rates and the use of delay terms as key trends in SARS-CoV-2 research, emphasizing the importance of theoretical models in guiding data analysis and the application of statistical methods. Furthermore, the paper discusses the challenges of accurately representing vaccine-driven reductions in infectiousness and the varying approaches to doing so within models. By examining both the mathematical frameworks and the data they aim to analyze, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic from a mathematical perspective, offering valuable insights for both researchers and policymakers. This viewpoint is intended to contribute to the development of a unified theoretical foundation to analyze and respond to emerging epidemics, encouraging collaboration across mathematical, epidemiological, and statistical disciplines. We present novel constructions for Golay complementary pairs over finite fields for vectors representing rotations of 0 and 360 degrees, as well as extensions to include vectors representing 120 and 180 degree rotations. A system for generating simulated brain lesions has been developed, consisting of a combination of a generative model and a discriminative model. The generative model, a progressive G-AE, creates an initial simulated lesion that is then refined by the discriminative model, a deep learning architecture, to produce a more realistic representation. This representation is ultimately used to concatenate with a healthy brain image, utilizing a patch-based technique to account for varying lesion sizes and locations. The proposed method has been tested on two publicly available datasets, and compared to existing simulated lesion generation techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness by obtaining the highest scores in two evaluation tasks. The development of this system addresses the need for large amounts of simulated brain lesion data, particularly for training machine learning models to detect lesions, with minimal requirement for real-world data.
